Surah al-Kahf (The Cave) is Meccan, though it has been said that the exception is His saying ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord﴾ and what follows, to the end of the verse. It has one hundred and eleven verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Praise be to Allah, who has sent down to His servant the Book﴾, meaning the Qur'an. He linked the due of praise to its being sent down, drawing attention to the fact that it is among His greatest blessings, because it is the guide to what perfects the servants and the caller to that by which the well-being of this life and the Hereafter is ordered.

﴿And has not made in it any crookedness﴾: no part of crookedness, either in disorder of wording or contradiction in meaning, or deviation from the call to the truth. In meanings, it is like crookedness in physical things.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 2–3:

﴿Upright﴾ (qayyiman): straight and balanced, with neither excess nor deficiency in it. Or, ﴿upright﴾ in regard to the welfare of the servants, so that it is a description of it as perfecting after its description as perfect. Or, it bears witness to the truth of the earlier books. Its accusative (intisab) is by an implied verb, whose estimated form is "He made it upright" (ja'alahu qayyiman), or it is in the state (hal) of the pronoun in ﴿for Him﴾, or it is a state of ﴿the Book﴾, on the basis that the wa' in ﴿and He has not made﴾ is for the state and not for conjunction (ataf). For if it were for conjunction, the conjoined element would separate parts of the conjoined-to element. For this reason it has been said that there is a fronting and deferring (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it. It has also been read as "qayyiman" (with fatha). ﴿To warn of a severe punishment﴾: that is, to warn those who disbelieve of a severe punishment. The first object has been omitted, being sufficiently indicated by the context and by restricting attention to the purpose being pursued. ﴿From Him﴾: proceeding from His presence. Abu Bakr read the dal with sukun, like the sukun of the ba' in the reading of Ibn Kathir? No: Abu Bakr [ʿAsim] read it with sukun on the dal, as the sukun of the ba', from among the seven readings, together with ishmam, to indicate its original vowel; with kasra on the nun because of the meeting of two sakin letters; and with kasra on the ha' by way of assimilation (ittiba'). ﴿And give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a good reward﴾: it is Paradise.

﴿Remaining therein﴾: in the reward. ﴿Forever﴾: without cessation.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 4–5:

﴿And warn those who say, "God has taken a son."﴾ He singled them out for mention and repeated the warning as it relates to them, magnifying their disbelief. He did not mention what they are warned against, because it had already been mentioned.

﴿They have no knowledge of it﴾, that is, of the son, or of taking one, or of the saying. The meaning is that they say it out of extreme ignorance and false supposition, or by imitating what they heard from their predecessors without knowing the sense in which those predecessors intended it. They used to apply the terms "father" and "son" to mean "the one who influences" and "the thing influenced." Or the meaning is: "nor do they know God," for if they knew Him they would not have permitted attributing the taking of a son to Him. ﴿Nor to their fathers﴾, those who first invented this saying, in the sense of (p-273) adoption (tabanni, the taking of a son by adoption). ﴿Grave is the word﴾, that is, their statement is great in disbelief, because of what it contains of likening God to creation, associating partners with Him, and suggesting that He has need of a son to help Him and succeed Him, along with other deviations. The word ﴿kalimatan﴾ (word) is in the accusative as a tamyiz (specification, an accusative noun clarifying the sense of the preceding word). It has also been read in the nominative as the agent, but the first reading is more eloquent and more indicative of the intended meaning. ﴿It comes out of their mouths﴾ is a description of it, conveying the magnitude of their audacity in letting it issue from their mouths. What actually emerges is the breath that carries it. It has also been said that the description belongs to an omitted subject, namely the one being dispraised, because "kabura" here carries the sense of "bi'sa" (how wretched). It has been read as "kabrat" with sukun (silent vowel) together with ishmam (a partial rounding of the lips, a recitation technique). ﴿They speak only falsehood﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 18, verse 6:

﴿فَلَعَلَّكَ باخِعٌ نَفْسَكَ﴾ *qātiluhā* (killing it). ﴿عَلى آثارِهِمْ﴾ *idhā tawallaw ʿani al-īmān* (when they turn away from faith). He compares him, because of the grief that enters him over their turning away, to one whose beloved ones have departed from him, so he grieves over their traces and destroys his own self out of sorrow for them. It is also read as «باخِعُ نَفْسِكَ» in the construct form (*ʿalā al-iḍāfa*). ﴿إنْ لَمْ يُؤْمِنُوا بِهَذا الحَدِيثِ﴾ *bihādhā al-Qurʾān* (with this Qur'an). ﴿أسَفًا﴾ is either for the sake of grieving over them (*li-l-taʾassuf*) or as a state: *mutaʾassifan ʿalayhim* (grieving over them). *Al-asaf* is an excess of sorrow and anger. It is also read «أنْ» with a fatḥa, as *li-anْ*, and then «باخِعٌ» may not govern (*iʿmāl*) unless it is taken as a narration of a past state (*ḥikāyat ḥāl māḍiya*).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 7–8:

﴿Indeed, We have made what is on the earth﴾ of animals, plants and minerals, ﴿an adornment for it﴾ and for its people, ﴿that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed﴾ in dealing with it. This is one who renounces it, is not deceived by it, is content with what sustains his days and spends it as is fitting. In this there is consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

﴿And indeed, We will surely make what is upon it a barren, dry ground﴾ — a warning against it. Juruz (barren, dry, cut-off) is the land whose vegetation has been cut off. It is derived from al-jarz (cutting off). The meaning is: indeed, We will reduce what is upon it of adornment to dust levelled with the earth, and make it like a smooth, bare surface (ṣaʿīd) with no vegetation in it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on Surah 18, verse 9:

﴿Or did you think﴾ rather, did you think? ﴿that the Companions of the Cave and the Inscription﴾ were, in keeping them alive for a long span of time. ﴿were among Our signs a wonder﴾. Their story, compared with the creation of the kinds and species on earth, which are too numerous to be counted, having widely differing natures and diverse forms that amaze the observers, all made from one substance, is not so wonderful in its return to that substance, although it is one of the signs of God, like a small, insignificant trifle. The *kahf* (cave) is a wide cavern in a mountain. *Al-Raqim* is the name of the mountain or the valley in which their cave lies, or the name of their town or their dog. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"There was nothing there but al-Raqim neighbouring them, and their hunting, while the folk in the cave slept."

Or it is a lead or stone tablet on which their names were inscribed and which was placed at the entrance of the cave. It has also been said that the Companions of al-Raqim were another people, who were "three who went out seeking provision for their families, and the sky seized them, so they took shelter in a cave, and a rock slid down and sealed its entrance. One of them said: Remember which of you has done a good deed, that perhaps God will have mercy on us for its sake. One of them said: I once hired labourers, and a man came in the middle of the day and worked for the rest of the day like them, so I gave him the same wage as theirs. One of them became angry and left his wage, so I put it aside in a corner of the house. Then cattle passed by me, and I bought with it a young cow, and it grew as God willed. After a time he came back to me as a weak old man, whom I did not recognise, and said: You owe me a debt; and he mentioned it to me until I recognised him, so I gave him all of it. O God, if I did that for Your sake, then relieve us. The mountain split until they saw the light. Another said: I had a surplus, and the people were struck by hardship. A woman came to me and asked me for a kindness. I said: By God, it is not less than your own self. She refused and returned, and came back three times. Then she mentioned it to her husband, and he said: Respond to her and relieve your dependants. So she came and gave herself to me. When I uncovered her and was about to approach her, she trembled. I said: What is wrong with you? She said: I fear God. I said to her: You feared Him in hardship and I did not fear Him in ease. So I left her and gave her what she sought. O God, if I did that for Your sake, then relieve us. It split until they recognised one another. The third said: I had two elderly parents, and I had sheep, and I used to feed and water my parents, then return to my sheep. One day rain detained me, and I did not leave until evening. I came to my family and took my milking pail and milked into it and went to them, but I found them asleep. I disliked waking them, so I remained sitting with the pail in my hands until dawn woke them, and I gave them to drink. O God, if I did that for Your sake, then relieve us. So God relieved them, and they came out." This was traced back (to the Prophet) by Nu'man ibn Bashir.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 10–11:

﴿When the youths took refuge in the cave﴾ meaning: youths from among the nobles of the Romans, whom Daqyanus (Decius) compelled to idolatry, but they refused and fled to the cave. ﴿And they said: Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself﴾ meaning: make forgiveness, provision and security from the enemy incumbent upon us. ﴿And prepare for us from our affair﴾ meaning: from the affair in which we are, namely separation from the disbelievers. ﴿Right guidance﴾ meaning: that by means of it we may become rightly guided and well-guided. Or, make our entire affair right guidance, as in your saying: "I saw from you a lion." The original meaning of tahayyi’ (preparation) is bringing about the form (hay'ah) of a thing.

﴿So We struck upon their ears﴾ meaning: We placed upon them a veil that prevents hearing, in the sense that We put them to sleep with a sleep in which sounds do not wake them. The object has been omitted, as it is omitted in their saying: "He built upon his wife." ﴿In the cave for years﴾ are two adverbial complements (zarfan) governed by "We struck."

﴿Counted﴾ meaning: possessing a number. The description of the years by this word admits of both multiplication and reduction, for the duration of their stay is, in His sight, like part of a day.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 12–13:

﴿Then We roused them﴾, meaning We woke them up. ﴿So that We might know﴾, meaning so that Our knowledge would relate to it in a present, actual manner that corresponds to its earlier relation, which was in the future tense. ﴿Which of the two parties﴾, the two disagreeing groups among them or among others, ﴿was best at reckoning﴾ the period of their stay. ﴿For what they had stayed, a term﴾: they preserved (ḍabaṭa) the length of the time of their stay. The interrogative sense in the word ﴿which﴾ has been suspended from the verb ﴿We might know﴾. So it (ayyu, "which") is the subject (mubtada, "subject of a nominal sentence"), and ﴿was best at reckoning﴾ (aḥṣā) is its predicate (khabar, "predicate of a nominal sentence"). It is a past-tense verb (fi'l māḍī). ﴿A term﴾ (amadan) is an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu, "object indicating the reason for the action"), and ﴿for what they had stayed﴾ (limā labithū) is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, "circumstantial qualifier") of it or an object of purpose. It has been said that it is the object, with the lām being superfluous and mā being a relative pronoun, and ﴿a term﴾ is a specifier (tamyīz, "accusative of specification"). It has also been said that aḥṣā is a superlative form (ism al-tafḍīl, "elative/comparative noun") from iḥṣā', with the extra letters removed, as in their saying: "He is more knowledgeable of wealth (aḥṣā lil-māl) and more bankrupt than the son of al-Mudhlaq." And ﴿a term﴾ is governed by a verb implied by aḥṣā, as in his saying:

"And I strike, among us, with swords the helmets."

﴿We narrate to you their story with truth﴾, with sincerity. ﴿Indeed they were youths﴾, young men, the plural of fatā, like ṣabiy and ṣibyah. ﴿They believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance﴾, through steadfastness.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 14–15:

﴿And We strengthened their hearts﴾ and fortified them with patience in forsaking homeland, family and wealth, and with boldness in proclaiming the truth and in confronting Decianus the tyrant. ﴿When they stood up﴾ before him, ﴿and said: "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We shall never call upon any god besides Him. Otherwise we would have uttered an outrageous thing."﴾ By Allah, we would have uttered a statement of outrage (shatat), meaning one far removed from the truth and excessive in wrongdoing.

(p-275) ﴿These our people﴾ is the subject (mubtada'). ﴿Our people﴾ is an explicative apposition (‘atf bayan). ﴿have taken besides Him gods﴾ is its predicate (khabar), and it is a statement carrying the sense of denunciation (inkar).

﴿Why do they not bring﴾ means: why do they not bring (halla yatun). ﴿against them﴾ means: for their worship. ﴿a clear authority﴾ means: a manifest proof, for religion is not taken except by it. This indicates that whatever religious creed lacks evidence is rejected, and that blind imitation (taqlid) in it is not permissible. ﴿Who is more wrong than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾ by ascribing a partner to Him?

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 18, verse 16:

﴿And when you withdraw from them﴾: this is the address of some of them to others. ﴿and what they worship, other than Allah﴾ is conjoined to the object pronoun, meaning: "and when you withdraw from the people and their deities, other than Allah, for they used to worship Allah and also worship idols, like the rest of the polytheists." It is permissible for (ما) (*ma*, here a *masdariyyah*, a particle that forms a verbal noun) to be read as meaning: "and when you withdraw from them and their worship, except the worship of Allah." It is also permissible for it to be a negating particle (*nafiyah*), in which case it is a statement from Allah, exalted is He, about the youths regarding monotheism, interposed between (إذ) (*idh*, "when") and its answer, to confirm their withdrawal.

﴿So take refuge in the cave; your Lord will spread out for you of His mercy﴾: He will extend provision for you and widen it upon you, ﴿of His mercy﴾ in both abodes. ﴿and will facilitate for you in your affair a means of ease (*mirfaq*)﴾: that by which you gain benefit, i.e., you derive advantage. Their certainty of this stems from the clarity of their conviction and the strength of their trust in the bounty of Allah, exalted is He.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿*mirfaqan*﴾ with a *fatha* on the *mim* and a *kasra* on the *fa'*. It is a verbal noun that came irregularly (*shadhdh*), like (*al-marji'*) and (*al-mahid*), since its regular pattern (*qiyas*) is with a *fatha*.

﴿And you would see the sun﴾: that is, if you had seen them. The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or to everyone.

﴿When it rises, it turns away from their cave to the right﴾: it inclines away from it, so that its rays do not fall on them and harm them, because the cave faced south, or because God Most High turned it away from them. Its original form is تَتَزاوَرُ (*tatazāwaru*), and the *tā'* was assimilated into the *zāy* (*idghām*, the merging of one consonant into the next). The Kufans read it with the *tā'* deleted, while Ibn 'Āmir and Ya'qūb read تَزْوَرُّ (*tazwarru*), like تَحْمَرُّ (*taḥmarru*). It was also read تَزْوارُّ (*tazwārru*), like تَحْمارُّ (*taḥmārru*). All of these derive from الزَّوْر (*al-zawr*), meaning inclination.

﴿to the right﴾ (ذاتَ اليَمِينِ): toward the direction of the right. Its literal sense is "the direction that has the name of the right."

﴿And when it sets, it passes them by on the left﴾ (تَقْرِضُهُمْ): it cuts across them and leaves them behind. ﴿On the left﴾ (ذاتَ الشِّمالِ): meaning the right and left sides of the cave, as in His saying: ﴿while they were in a spacious place within it﴾, that is, while they were in a wide space within the cave, namely in its middle, such that the breeze reaches them, the closeness of the cave does not harm them, and the heat of the sun does not harm them. This is because the entrance of the cave faces the Pleiades (بَناتِ نَعْشٍ, *banāt Na'sh*), and the nearest of the risings and settings to its alignment is the rising and setting point of the head of Cancer (السَّرَطان). When the sun's orbit is its orbit, it rises inclining away from the cave, facing its right side, which is the side nearer the west, and it sets facing its left side, so that its rays fall on both sides. It dissipates the cave's foulness, moderates its air, and does not fall on them in a way that would harm their bodies or wear out their clothes.

﴿That is among the signs of God﴾: that is, their condition and their sheltering in a cave of such a nature are among the signs of God, or your relating their story is, or the sun's turning away from them and passing them by as it rises and sets is among the signs of God.

﴿Whomever God guides﴾: by granting success.

﴿He is the one guided﴾: the one who has attained success. What is meant by this is either praise of them, or an alert that signs like these are numerous, but the one who benefits from them is the one whom God has enabled to reflect on them and to gain insight through them.

﴿And whomever He leaves astray﴾: whomever He forsakes.

﴿And you would think them awake﴾ because their eyes were open, or because of how often they turned over. ﴿while they were asleep﴾, sleeping. ﴿And We turned them﴾ during their sleep.

(p-276) ﴿to the right and to the left﴾ so that the earth would not consume the parts of their bodies that lie adjacent to it over the long period of time. It was also read *taqallubahum* as a verbal noun (*masdar*) in the accusative, governed by a verb implied by *tahsabuhum*, meaning "and you see their turning." ﴿And their dog﴾ was a dog that passed by them, followed them, and was driven away by them. Then Allah, the Exalted, made it speak, and it said: "I am the most beloved of Allah's beloved ones. So sleep, and I will guard you." Or it was the dog of a shepherd who passed by them, followed them, and the dog followed them too. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 19–20:

﴿And thus did We raise them up﴾: just as We put them to sleep as a sign, We raised them up as a sign of the perfection of Our power. ﴿That they might question one another﴾: so that some of them would ask others, and thus they would learn their condition and what Allah had done with them, and so they would increase in certainty regarding the perfection of Allah's power, would take from it insight into the matter of resurrection (al-ba'th), and would give thanks for the blessing Allah had bestowed upon them. ﴿A speaker among them said: "How long have you remained?" They said: "We have remained a day or part of a day."﴾ This was based on their most probable assessment, because one who sleeps cannot count the duration of his sleep, and for this reason they referred knowledge to Allah, exalted is He. ﴿They said: "Your Lord knows best how long you have remained."﴾ It is also possible that this was the statement of some of them, and that this was the denial of the others against them. It was also said that they entered the cave in the morning (ghudwah) and awoke in the afternoon (zahirah), and they thought that they were in their same day or the day after it, and so they said that. Then, when they looked at the length of their nails and hair, they said: "This [is more than a day]." Then, when they knew that the matter was unclear and that they had no way to knowledge of it, they turned to what concerned them and said: ﴿"So send one of you with this silver of yours to the city."﴾ Al-warq is silver, whether minted or unminted. Abu Bakr, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and Rawh on the authority of Ya'qub read it with the light pronunciation (al-takhfif). It was also read with the heavy pronunciation (al-tathqil), with the qaf assimilated into the kaf, and with the light pronunciation with a kasra on the waw, both assimilated and unassimilated. The assimilated form was rejected because of the meeting of two sukun-bearing letters, contrary to its normal rule. Their taking of provisions with them is evidence that provisioning is the view of those who rely upon Allah (al-mutawakkilun). The city (al-madinah) is Tarsus. ﴿"Then let him look which of them has the purest food"﴾: which of its people has the purest food, ﴿azka ta'aman﴾: the most lawful and most wholesome, or the most abundant and the cheapest. ﴿"Let him bring you provision from it, and let him be gentle"﴾: let him take special care in dealing so that he is not defrauded, or in concealing himself so that he is not recognized. ﴿"And let him not make anyone aware of you"﴾: and let him not do anything that leads to awareness.

﴿"For if they come to know of you"﴾: that is, if they discover you or prevail over you; the pronoun refers to the people implied in ﴿ayyuha﴾. ﴿"they will stone you"﴾: they will kill you by stoning. ﴿"or return you to their religion"﴾: or make you return to it against your will, with "return" (y'ud) meaning "become" (al-sayrurah). It was also said that they had originally been upon their religion and then believed. ﴿"And you will never prosper, then, ever"﴾: if you enter into their religion.

﴿They will say﴾, that is, those who dispute about their story in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ), from among the People of the Book and the believers. ﴿They are three, and their fourth is their dog﴾, that is, they are three men, and their dog makes them four by joining them. It was said that this is the saying of the Jews, and it was said that it is the saying of the chief (al-sayyid) of the Christians of Najran, who was a Ya'qubi (Jacobite). ﴿And they say, they are five, and their sixth is their dog﴾, said by the Christians, or by al-'Aqib among them, who was a Nestorian. ﴿Conjecturing about the unseen﴾, they cast at it (ramy) a report that is hidden, of which they have no access, and they bring it forth; or it means a guess about the unseen, from their saying "rajama bi'l-zann" when one guesses. The word is not given with the particle "bi" (in the form "rajman bi'l-ghayb" with the sin), because it is sufficient to join it to what it is part of (i.e., the preceding clause). ﴿And they say, they are seven, and their eighth is their dog﴾. This was said only by the Muslims, on the report of the Messenger (ﷺ) to them about Gabriel, peace be upon them both, and by God Most High's indication to him, by following it with His saying: ﴿Say: My Lord knows best their number; none knows them but a few﴾. He followed the first two sayings with His saying: ﴿conjecturing about the unseen﴾, and by establishing knowledge of them for a group after He had limited the sayings of the groups to the three mentioned. For the non-mention of a fourth in such a context is evidence of its non-existence, while the principle also negates it. Then He rejected the first two by following them with His saying: ﴿conjecturing about the unseen﴾, so that the third becomes definite. And by His placing the conjunction "wa" (and) before the clause that comes as an attribute of an indefinite noun, likening it to a clause that comes as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of a definite noun, to emphasize the adherence of the attribute to the thing described and to indicate that its being described by it is a fixed matter.

It is related from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, that they were seven, and their eighth was their dog. Their names: Yamlikha, Maksalinia and Mashlinia, these are the companions of the king's right hand; Marnush, Dabranush and Shadhanush, the companions of his left, and he used to consult them; and the seventh was the shepherd who agreed with them. The name of their dog was Qitmir, and the name of their city was Afsus.

It was also said that the three sayings belong to the People of the Book and to a few of them. ﴿So do not dispute about them except with an outward dispute﴾, so do not argue concerning the matter of the youths except with an outward argument, not going deep into it, and this is that you recite to them what is in the Qur'an without making them ignorant (of their error) and without refuting them. ﴿And do not seek a ruling about them from any of them﴾, and do not ask any of them about their story as one seeking guidance, for in what has been revealed to you there is sufficiency apart from it, while they have no knowledge of it. Nor (should you ask) as one seeking to embarrass, wishing to expose the one questioned and to show up what he has as false, for that corrupts the noble morals.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 23–24:

﴿And do not say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow,"﴾ ﴿unless [you add], "If Allah wills."﴾ This is a prohibition of discipline from Allah, the Exalted, to His Prophet, when the Jews said to the Quraysh: "Ask him about the Spirit, the People of the Cave, and Dhu al-Qarnayn." They asked him, and he said: "Come to me tomorrow and I will inform you," and he did not make the exception (istithna'). So the revelation was delayed for some fifteen days, until it grieved him and the Quraysh called him a liar. The exception (istithna', lit. "saying 'if Allah wills'") is from the prohibition, meaning: do not say, concerning something you resolve upon, "Indeed I will do it in the future," except with ﴿"If Allah wills"﴾, i.e., except while being associated with His will, saying "If Allah wills," or except at the time when Allah wills that you say it, in the sense that He permits you to do so. It is not permissible to attach it (the exception) to the act itself, because the exception of the will's accompanying the act is not sound, and the exception of its being placed before it does not suit the prohibition. ﴿And remember your Lord﴾ — the will of your Lord — ﴿and say, "If Allah wills."﴾ It is narrated that when this was revealed, he (ﷺ) said: "If Allah wills."

﴿When you forget﴾ — when you have forgotten this and then remember it. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "Even after a year, so long as one has not broken the oath (yahnath)." For this reason he permitted delaying the exception after the statement. But the majority of jurists (fuqaha') hold otherwise, because if that were valid, no acknowledgment (iqrar), divorce (talaq), or manumission ('itaq) would ever be fixed, and the truthfulness or falsehood of a statement would never be known. Neither the verse nor the report indicates that the exception made after the fact is attached to the preceding statement; rather, it is from an implied omitted element indicated by it. It is also possible that the meaning is: "Remember your Lord with glorification and seeking forgiveness when you forget the exception," emphasizing the urging to it; or "Remember your Lord and His punishment when you have left some of what He commanded you, so that it moves you to make amends"; or "Remember Him when forgetfulness overtakes you, so that He reminds you of what was forgotten."

﴿And say, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me﴾ — will direct me — ﴿to what is nearer to this in right guidance (rashad)."﴾ That is, to what is nearer in right guidance and clearer as a proof that I am a prophet than the account of the People of the Cave. He has indeed guided him to something greater than that, such as the stories of the prophets whose times were distant from his, and the informing of unseen matters and events that will occur in future ages until the Hour arrives. Or the meaning is: "to what is nearer in right guidance and closer in good than what was forgotten."

**Verse 25: "And they remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine."**

"That is, their stay in it while alive, with their ears struck (so that they could not hear), and this is an elucidation of what was stated in summary before." And it has been said that it is a report of the speech of the People of the Book, for they differed concerning the duration of their stay just as they differed concerning their number. Some of them said "three hundred," and some of them said "three hundred and nine years."

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "*thalath mi'atin*" (three hundreds) with the genitive construction (*idafa*), placing the plural in the position of the singular. What makes this preferable here is that the plural marker in it compensates for what was omitted from the singular, and that the original rule for numbers is that they are construed with a plural noun. Whoever did not read it with the *idafa* made *sinin* (years) an apposition (*badal*) to *thalath mi'a* (three hundred).

﴿Say: "Allah knows best how long they stayed. To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth."﴾ That is, to Him belongs whatever is hidden within them and whatever is concealed of the conditions of their inhabitants. Therefore no creature is hidden from Him in knowledge.

﴿See how clearly He sees and hears!﴾ It is mentioned in the form of wonder (ta'ajjub, expressing amazement) to indicate that His perception is beyond that of all hearers and seers, since nothing veils Him from anything, and the subtle and the dense, the small and the great, and the hidden and the manifest do not differ before Him. The pronoun (al-ha', "him") refers to Allah, and its position is in the nominative (raf') as the agent (fa'iliyya). The bi' (ba', "with") is redundant (mazida) according to Sibawayh, and the original form was abṣara, meaning "he became one who has sight." Then it was transferred to the imperative form with the meaning of creating a statement (inshā'), so the pronoun appeared either because the form is not suitable for Him, or because of the redundancy of the ba', as in His saying ﴿And sufficient is He﴾. The accusative (naṣb) is as the object (maf'uliyya) according to al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash, "the Younger"), and the agent is the pronoun of the one addressed, who is everyone, and the ba' is redundant if the hamza is for transitivity, and transitive (mu'addiya) if the hamza is for becoming.

﴿They have no protector besides Him﴾: the pronoun refers to the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth. ﴿No ally﴾: one who manages their affairs.

﴿And He does not make anyone a partner in His command﴾: in His judgment. ﴿anyone﴾ among them, nor does He grant anyone any entry into it.

Ibn 'Amir and Qalun from Ya'qub read with the ta' (taa', "you") and the jazm (jazm, the apocopate mood) as a prohibition (nahy) of everyone from associating partners. Then, when the content of the Qur'an, through the story of the People of the Cave, indicated, insofar as it is among the unseen matters in relation to the Messenger (ﷺ), that it is a miraculous revelation (wahy mu'jiz), He commanded him to persist in his study and to keep company with his companions, and so He said:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 27–28:

﴿And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord﴾ of the Qur'an, and do not heed their saying: ﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it.﴾

﴿None can change His words﴾ no one other than Him is able to alter or change them. ﴿And you will not find any refuge other than Him﴾ a place of refuge to resort to, should you intend it.

﴿And restrain yourself﴾ hold yourself back and steady yourself. ﴿with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾ in the gatherings of their times, or at the two ends of the day. Ibn 'Amir read ﴿bil-ghudwah﴾ (with the definite article in the singular form). In this reading, ghudwah is mostly a proper noun (a fixed name for a time of day), so the lam in it is taken as a lam of indefinite sense (ta'wil al-tankir).

﴿Seeking His Face﴾ seeking the good pleasure of Allah and His obedience. ﴿And let not your eyes pass beyond them﴾ let your gaze not go beyond them to others. The verb is followed by ʿan because it is taken to include the sense of "to turn away from" (tadmin ma'na naba'). It has also been read as ﴿wa la ta'du 'aynaka﴾ and ﴿wa la tu'addi﴾ from a'dahu and 'addahu. The intended meaning is the prohibition to the Messenger ﷺ from looking down on the poor believers and letting his eye rise above their shabby dress out of eagerness for the splendour of the attire of the wealthy. ﴿Desiring the adornment of the worldly life﴾ a circumstantial clause (hal) from the kaf (the pronoun "you") in the well-known reading, and from the hidden pronoun in the verb in other readings. ﴿And do not obey him whose heart We have made heedless﴾ whose heart We have made unmindful.

﴿of Our remembrance﴾ such as Umayyah ibn Khalaf, in your invitation to drive away the poor from your assembly for the chiefs of Quraysh. In this there is an indication that what calls him to this request is the heedlessness of his heart toward intelligible realities and his absorption in sensible things, to the point that he failed to perceive that honour lies in the adornment of the soul, not in the adornment of the body, and that if he obeyed him he would be like him in foolishness. The Mu'tazilah, when the attribution of making heedless to Allah the Exalted troubled them, said: it is like "ajbantuhu" (I found him a coward) when one finds him so, or its attribution to Him; or it is from "aghfala ibilahu" (he left his camels without a mark), i.e., We did not mark him with Our remembrance, like the hearts of those in whose hearts We wrote faith. They argued that the intended meaning is not the apparent sense of what was mentioned first in His words: ﴿and followed his desire﴾; and the answer to them is what has passed more than once. It has also been read as ﴿aghfalna﴾ with the verb attributed to the heart, in the sense that We reckoned his heart as heedless of His remembrance of him by way of punishment. ﴿And his affair was excess﴾ that is, transgression beyond the truth and casting it behind his back. It is said: "a horse that is a faras (a foremost one)" meaning one going ahead of the horses, and from this comes "al-faraṭ" (the one who goes ahead to prepare the way).

The intended meaning is the prohibition to the Messenger ﷺ from looking down on the poor believers and letting his eye rise above their shabby dress out of eagerness for the splendour of the attire of the wealthy. ﴿Desiring the adornment of the worldly life﴾ a circumstantial clause (hal) from the kaf (the pronoun "you") in the well-known reading, and from the hidden pronoun in the verb in other readings. ﴿And do not obey him whose heart We have made heedless﴾ whose heart We have made unmindful.

﴿of Our remembrance﴾ such as Umayyah ibn Khalaf, in your invitation to drive away the poor from your assembly for the chiefs of Quraysh. In this there is an indication that what calls him to this request is the heedlessness of his heart toward intelligible realities and his absorption in sensible things, to the point that he failed to perceive that honour lies in the adornment of the soul, not in the adornment of the body, and that if he obeyed him he would be like him in foolishness. The Mu'tazilah, when the attribution of making heedless to Allah the Exalted troubled them, said: it is like "ajbantuhu" (I found him a coward) when one finds him so, or its attribution to Him; or it is from "aghfala ibilahu" (he left his camels without a mark), i.e., We did not mark him with Our remembrance, like the hearts of those in whose hearts We wrote faith. They argued that the intended meaning is not the apparent sense of what was mentioned first in His words: ﴿and followed his desire﴾; and the answer to them is what has passed more than once. It has also been read as ﴿aghfalna﴾ with the verb attributed to the heart, in the sense that We reckoned his heart as heedless of His remembrance of him by way of punishment. ﴿And his affair was excess﴾ that is, transgression beyond the truth and casting it behind his back. It is said: "a horse that is a faras (a foremost one)" meaning one going ahead of the horses, and from this comes "al-faraṭ" (the one who goes ahead to prepare the way).

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 29:**

﴿Say, "The truth is from your Lord."﴾ The truth is what comes from God, not what desire dictates. It is also permissible for *al-ḥaqq* (the truth) to be the predicate (*khabar*, the predicate of a nominal sentence) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*, the subject of a nominal sentence), and ﴿from your Lord﴾ to be a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*, a phrase describing the state of the subject at the time of the action). ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve.﴾ I am not concerned with the faith of the one who believes, nor with the disbelief of the one who disbelieves. This does not imply that the servant independently determines his act, for although it is by his will, his will is not by his own will.

﴿We have prepared﴾ (p-280) means "We have readied." ﴿for the wrongdoers a Fire, whose enclosure surrounds them.﴾ *Surādiquhā* means its tent (*fusṭāṭuhā*). It is likened to the Fire that surrounds them. It has been said that *al-surādiq* is the chamber that lies around the tent. It has also been said that its enclosure is its smoke, and it has been said that it is a wall of fire. ﴿And if they plead for water﴾ from thirst, ﴿they will be given water like molten metal﴾, that is, like melted flesh. It has been said that it is like the dregs of oil, and this is in the manner of the poet's saying: *fa-u'tibū bi'l-Ṣaylam* ("so they were requited with al-Ṣaylam"). ﴿It scalds the faces﴾, for when it is brought near to be drunk, the intensity of its heat scalds them. This is a second description (*ṣifa*, an adjective or qualifying description) of *māʾ* (water), or a circumstantial clause from *al-muhl* (molten metal), or from the pronoun (*ḍamīr*, pronoun) in the *kāf* (the letter *kāf*, "like").

﴿Wretched is the drink﴾, namely the molten metal. ﴿And evil is the resting place﴾, namely the Fire. ﴿A couch (*murtafaqan*)﴾ means a reclining place. The basic meaning of *al-irtifāq* is placing the elbow under the cheek. This is in contrast to His saying ﴿and good is the resting place﴾, for otherwise the people of the Fire have no resting.

Verse 30 of Surah al-Kahf: "Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds—indeed, We do not allow to be lost the reward of one who has done good in deed."

The predicate of the first "inna" (indeed) is the second clause together with what is within its scope. The returning pronoun (al-raji') is omitted; its estimated form is "who has done good in deed among them," or it is dispensed with by the generality of "one who has done good in deed," just as it is dispensed with in your saying: "How excellent a man is Zayd" (ni'ma al-rajul Zayd). Or it stands in the place of an apparent noun, for "one who has done good in deed" cannot correctly be applied in its literal sense except to those who have believed and done righteous deeds.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 31:

﴿Those, theirs are the Gardens of Eden, through which rivers flow beneath them.﴾ What lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraḍ). According to the first reading, it is a fresh resumption (isti'naf) to explain the reward, or it is a second predicate (khabar thani). ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾. The ﴿min﴾ in the first place is for the beginning of the source (li'l-ibtida'), and the second is for explanation (li'l-bayan), describing ﴿bracelets﴾. Its being indefinite (tankir) is to magnify the beauty of what encircles the wrist, and it is the plural of ʾaswira or ʾaswar, as the plural of siwar (bracelet). ﴿And they will wear green garments﴾, because green is the most beautiful of colours and the most fresh. ﴿Of fine green silk and brocade﴾: cushions of dibaj (brocade silk), and what is thick of it. He combined the two kinds to indicate that therein is what the souls desire and the eyes delight in. ﴿Reclining therein upon couches﴾, on thrones, as is the posture of those who live in luxury. ﴿How excellent a reward﴾: the Garden and its bliss. ﴿And how good a resting place﴾: a place of reclining (muttaka').

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 32:

﴿And strike for them a parable﴾ of the disbeliever and the believer. ﴿Two men﴾: the state of two men, either imagined or existing, who are two brothers from the Children of Israel: a disbeliever named Qatrus and a believer named Yahudha. They inherited from their father eight thousand dinars and divided them equally. The disbeliever spent his share on estates and property, while the believer spent his in the ways of good. Their affair ended as Allah the Exalted has related. It is also said that the two being presented as a parable were two brothers from the Banu Makhzum: the disbeliever was al-Aswad ibn Abd al-Asad, and the believer was Abu Salama Abdullah, husband of Umm Salama before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿We made for one of them two gardens﴾, that is, two orchards. ﴿Of grapevines﴾, that is, of vineyards; and the whole clause is either an explanation of the parable or a description of the two men. ﴿And We surrounded them with palm trees﴾: We made the palm trees encircle them, enclosing their vineyards with them. It is said: "Hafahu al-qawm" when the people surrounded him, and "hafafthu-hu bihim" when I made them encircle him; so the particle "bi" makes the second object, as in your saying: "ghashitu-hu bihi" (I covered him with it). ﴿And We placed between them﴾: in the middle of them both.

﴿Crops﴾, so that each of them would comprise foodstuffs and fruits, continuously cultivated, in a good form and an elegant arrangement.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 33–34:

﴿Both gardens brought forth their produce﴾ — their fruit. The singular pronoun is used because "kilta" (both) is grammatically singular in form. It was also read as "Kull al-jannatayn atā ukulahu" (each of the two gardens brought forth its produce).

﴿and did not fail in it﴾ — did not diminish from its produce. ﴿in anything﴾ — which is customary in all other orchards, for fruit usually comes to completion in one year and falls short in another.

﴿And We caused a river to gush forth between them﴾ — so that their irrigation would endure, for that is the basis, and their splendor would increase. From Ya'qub, it is read "wa-fajjarnā" with the lighter form (takhfif).

﴿And he had abundant wealth﴾ — kinds of property besides the two gardens, from the verb "thammara" (he multiplied his wealth) when he increased it. ʿĀṣim read it with a fatḥah on the thā' and the mīm; Abū ʿAmr with a ḍammah on the thā' and sukūn on the mīm; and the rest with ḍammah on both. Likewise in His words ﴿and his fruit was encompassed﴾.

﴿So he said to his companion while he was disputing with him﴾ — arguing with him in speech, from "ḥāra" (he returned), meaning he went back and forth in discussion.

﴿I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in men﴾ — in retinue and helpers. It is said that it means sons who are male, because they are the ones who go forth (yanfuruna) with him.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 35–36:**

﴿And he entered his garden﴾, going about with his companion within it and boasting to him of it. The singular "garden" (jannah) is used because what is meant is his garden and what he had been given of worldly enjoyment, as a warning that he has no garden other than this one, and no share in the garden promised to the God-fearing (al-muttaqun). Or it is because each of his two gardens was joined to the other; or because the entering was into each one separately. ﴿And he was wronging himself﴾, harming himself through his self-admiration (ʿujb) and his disbelief. ﴿He said: I do not think that this will ever perish﴾, that it will come to an end, ﴿this﴾ garden, ﴿ever﴾, because of the length of his hope, the persistence of his heedlessness, and his being deceived by the respite given to him.

﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established﴾, coming to pass. ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord﴾ by resurrection, as you claim, ﴿I will surely find better than these﴾ than his garden. The two Hijazi readers and al-Shami read "minhuma" (from both of them), meaning from the two gardens. ﴿As a return﴾, a place of return and an outcome, because this one is perishable and that one is everlasting. He swore to this because he believed that God had bestowed upon him what He had bestowed only because he deserved it and merited it in himself, and He is with him wherever he turns.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 37–38:

﴿He said to him, his companion, while he was disputing with him: Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust﴾. Because it is the origin of your material, or the material of your origin. ﴿Then from a drop of semen﴾, for it is your nearer material. ﴿Then He proportioned you into a man﴾, then He balanced you and perfected you as a human being, male, mature, reaching the stage of men. He made his disbelief in the resurrection a disbelief in God Most High, because its source is doubt concerning the perfect power of God Most High. For this reason He arranged the denial upon His creating him from dust, for whoever is able to originate his creation from it is able to restore him from it.

﴿But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I do not associate anyone with my Lord﴾. Its original form is "lakinna ana", the alif of hamza was dropped by transferring the vowel (naql) or without it, so the two nuns came together and assimilation (idgham) occurred. Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub, in one transmission, read it with an alif in connected speech, either as compensation for the hamza or to treat connected speech as if pausing (idjra' al-wasl majra al-waqf). It has also been read as "lakinna ana" in its original form, where the pronoun is a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and the clause that follows as its predicate is the predicate of "ana"; or the pronoun refers to "Allah", with "Allah" in apposition to it, "my Lord" being its predicate, and the whole clause the predicate of "ana". The istidrak (corrective contrast) is with "Did you disbelieve", as if he said: "You are a disbeliever in Allah, but I am a believer in Him." It has also been read as "lakinna huwa Allahu rabbi, wa lakin ana la ilaha illa huwa rabbi".

﴿So perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden﴾ in this world or in the Hereafter, because of my faith. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 44:

﴿There﴾ (hunālika), in that station and that state. ﴿Authority belongs to God, the True﴾ (al-walāyatu lillāhi al-ḥaqq): the support belongs to Him alone, and none other is able to provide it, in accordance with His saying ﴿and he had no company to support him﴾, or [it means] He supports His believing friends against the disbelievers in it, as He supported, in what He did, the believer (his brother) against the disbeliever. His saying ﴿He is best in reward and best in outcome﴾ strengthens this, i.e., for His friends. Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read it with a kasra (al-walāyati), and its meaning is sovereignty and kingship, i.e., there sovereignty belongs to Him; it cannot be overcome, nor can anyone prevent Him, or [it means] none other is worshipped, like His exalted saying ﴿So when they board the ship, they call upon God, sincerely devoting religion to Him﴾. Thus it is a warning that His saying ﴿Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord﴾ was out of compulsion and distress at what had befallen him.

It was said: ﴿There﴾ refers to the Hereafter. Abū ʿAmr and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿al-ḥaqq﴾ with a ḍamma (al-ḥaqqu) as an attribute of ﴿al-walāyah﴾, and it was also read with a fatḥa (al-ḥaqqa) as an emphatic infinitive (maṣdar mu'akkad). ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah read ﴿ʿuqban﴾ with a sukūn, and it was read ʿuqbā; all of them carry the meaning of "outcome" (al-ʿāqibah).

(p-283) ﴿And strike for them the example of the life of this world﴾: Mention to them what resembles the life of this world in its splendour and the swiftness of its passing, or in its strange nature. ﴿Like water﴾: it is like water. It is also permissible that it be a second object of (اضرب, idrib, "strike"), with the meaning of صَيَّرَ (sayyara, "make/render"). ﴿We sent down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingled with it﴾: so the plants became intertwined by means of it, and some of them mixed with others because of its abundance and density; or it soaked into the plants until they were watered and flourished. On this reading the original form would have been "fakhtalata bi-nabati al-ard" (the water mingled with the plants of the earth), but since each of the two things mingled was described by the attribute of the other, the order was reversed for emphasis on its abundance. ﴿Then it became dry stalks﴾: broken, shattered. ﴿Which the winds scatter﴾: they disperse it. It was also read as "tudhrihi" (تُذْرِيهِ), from adhra. The thing being compared is neither the water nor its state alone, but the configuration drawn from the whole sentence: the state of plants that grow by water, being green and luxuriant, then becoming dry stalks that the winds blow away, so that they become as though they had never been. ﴿And Allah is over all things﴾: of bringing into being and bringing to an end.

﴿Capable (muqtadiran)﴾: able (qadiran).

The wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world. (Al-Baydawi's gloss:) Man adorns himself with them in his worldly life, and they pass away from him after a short while.

And the enduring good deeds: the righteous works of goodness whose reward remains for him forever, and included in them are what has been explained as the five daily prayers, the acts of Hajj, the fasting of Ramadan, "Subhan Allah" (Glory be to God), "al-hamdu lillah" (praise be to God), "la ilaha illa Allah" (there is no god but God), "Allahu akbar" (God is greatest), and good speech.

Better in the sight of your Lord in reward, and better in hope.

Because whoever does them will, in the Hereafter, obtain through them what he used to hope for through them in this world.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 47:

﴿And the day We set the mountains in motion﴾ Remember the day We uproot them and set them moving through the air, or We make them go away and turn them into scattered dust (haba'an munbaththan). It is permissible for this to be coordinated (ʿatf) with ﴿with your Lord﴾, meaning: the enduring good deeds are better in the sight of God and on the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and Ibn ʿAmir read (tusayyaru) with the ta' and in the passive voice (al-bina' lil-maf'ul), and it has also been read as ﴿tasir﴾ from sarat. ﴿And you see the earth laid bare﴾ badiyah (exposed), split open from beneath the mountains, with nothing on it to cover it; it has also been read as ﴿wa-tura﴾ in the passive form (bina' al-maf'ul). ﴿And We gather them﴾ and We assemble them at the place of standing (al-mawqif). Its coming in the past tense after ﴿We set in motion﴾ and ﴿you see﴾ is either to affirm the certainty of the gathering, or to indicate that their gathering takes place before the moving of the mountains, so that they may witness and observe what was promised to them; according to this, the waw is for the circumstantial clause (lil-hal) with qad implied. ﴿So We leave out not﴾ so We do not leave behind. ﴿Any one of them﴾ It is said: ghadarahu and aghdarahu, when he left it behind; from it come al-ghadr (betrayal), for leaving off fulfilment of a pledge, and al-ghadir (a pool), for what the flood has left behind. It has also been read with the ya' (yughadir).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 48–49:

﴿And they will be presented before your Lord⦆ He likened their state to that of soldiers presented before a sovereign, not so that he may recognize them, but so that he may give orders concerning them.

﴿Rows (ṣaffan)⦆ Arranged in lines, such that no one shields anyone else. ﴿Indeed you have come to Us⦆ with an implied "saying" (al-ḍimār al-qawl, i.e., an understood verb of speech), in a manner that makes it either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) or a governing element for "the Day We set in motion" (yawma nusayyir). ﴿Just as We created you the first time⦆ naked, with nothing of wealth or children with you, as in His saying: ﴿And you have come to Us alone, as We created you the first time⦆ [see Qur'an 6:94]. Or [it means] alive, like your first creation, in accordance with His saying: ﴿Rather, you claimed that We would never appoint for you an appointed time⦆, meaning a time for the fulfillment of the promise of resurrection and rising, and that the prophets had lied to you about it. "Rather" (bal) here serves to move from one narrative to another.

﴿And the Book will be placed⦆ the records of deeds placed in the right hands and the left hands, or in the scale; and it was said that it is a metaphor for the placing of the reckoning. ﴿So you will see the criminals fearful⦆ afraid. ﴿Of what is in it⦆ of the sins. ﴿And they will say, "Woe to us!"⦆ they call out for their destruction, which they brought upon themselves among all destructions. ﴿What sort of book is this⦆ in wonder at its condition. ﴿It leaves out no small thing⦆ no small detail. ﴿Nor any great thing but it has enumerated it⦆ except that it has counted it and encompassed it. ﴿And they will find what they did present⦆ written in the scrolls. ﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone⦆ by recording against him what he did not do, or by increasing his punishment beyond what fits his deed.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 50:

﴿And [mention] when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," so they prostrated, except Iblis﴾ He repeated it in several places because it is an introduction to matters whose explanation is intended in those contexts. Here, when He condemned those who boast and denounced their conduct, He affirmed that this is among the practices of Iblis. Or, when He explained the condition of the one deluded by the world and the one who turns away from it, and the cause of being deluded by it was love of desires and the whisperings of Satan, He first made them abstain from the adornments of the world, [explaining] that it is subject to decline, while righteous deeds are better and more lasting than them and more elevated. Then He turned them away from Satan by reminding them of the ancient enmity between them. This is the method of every repetition in the Qur'an. ﴿He was of the jinn﴾ is a circumstantial clause with "qad" understood, or a resumptive clause giving the reason, as if it were said: "What is the matter with him that he did not prostrate?" So it was said: "He was of the jinn." ﴿So he defied the command of his Lord﴾ so he departed from His command by abandoning prostration. The "fa" indicates causation. In this is evidence that the angel never disobeys at all, and that Iblis disobeyed only because he was originally of the jinn. The thorough discussion of this is in Surah al-Baqarah. ﴿Will you then take him﴾ after what has proceeded from him, "you take him" [as a guardian], and the hamza is for denunciation and wonder. ﴿And his offspring﴾ his children or his followers, and He called them offspring metaphorically. ﴿as allies instead of Me﴾ so that you substitute them for Me and obey them instead of obeying Me. ﴿While they are an enemy to you. Wretched is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾ from Allah, Most High: Iblis and his offspring.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 18, verse 51:**

﴿I did not make them witnesses to the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor to the creation of themselves.﴾ This negates that Iblis and his offspring were present at the creation of the heavens and the earth, and that some of them were present at the creation of others. The purpose is to indicate the negation of seeking support (*i'tiḍād*, taking someone as a helper) from them in that matter, as he stated explicitly in His words: ﴿Nor would I have taken the misleaders as helpers (*ʿaḍudan*)﴾, meaning as aides. This is a rejection of taking them as allies besides God, as partners to Him in worship. The entitlement to worship follows from creatorship (*al-khāliqiyya*), and sharing in creatorship necessitates sharing in worship. He placed "the misleaders" in the position of the pronoun, as a censure of them and a declaration that seeking their support is unlikely.

It was also said that the pronoun refers to the polytheists, and the meaning is: I did not make them witnesses to the creation of that, nor did I single them out with knowledge that no one else knows, such that if they believed, people would follow them, as they claim. So do not heed their words out of hope for their support of the religion, for it is not fitting for me to seek support from the misleaders for my religion. This is reinforced by the reading of the one who read (﴿وَما كُنْتَ﴾, "nor were you") in the address to the Messenger ﷺ. It was also read "*muttakhidhan al-muḍillīn*" (﴿مُتَّخِذًا المُضِلِّينَ﴾) in the original form, "*ʿaḍadan*" (﴿عَضُدًا﴾) with the sound lightened, "*ʿuḍudan*" (﴿عُضُدًا﴾) with the vowel assimilated to the following letter, and "*ʿaḍadan*" (﴿عَضَدًا﴾) like *khadam*, the plural of *ʿāḍid* (helper), from *ʿaḍadahu*, meaning he strengthened him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 52:

﴿And on the Day when He will say﴾: that is, Allah, the Exalted, to the disbelievers. Hamza recited it with the nun (﴿نقول﴾, "We will say"). ﴿"Call upon My partners whom you claimed"﴾ to be My partners and your intercessors, so that they may protect you from My punishment. The attribution of "partners" is according to their own assumption, for rebuke. What is meant is whatever was worshipped besides Him, and it has been said that it refers to Iblis and his offspring. ﴿"So they will call upon them"﴾, that is, they will call out to them for help. ﴿"But they will not respond to them"﴾, that is, they will not give them aid. ﴿"And We will place between them"﴾, between the disbelievers and their deities. ﴿"A barrier (mawbiqan)"﴾, a place of destruction in which they share, which is the Fire; or enmity which, in its severity, is a destruction, like the saying of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "Let not your love be excessive, nor your hatred destructive." Mawbiqan is either a noun of place or a verbal noun from waqa, yawqu, waqan, meaning "to perish." It has also been said that al-bayn means connection, i.e., and We will make their mutual connection in this world a destruction on the Day of Resurrection.(p-285)

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 53–54:**

﴿And the guilty will see the Fire and will know [with certainty]⁠﴾ — *fa-azannu* is glossed as *fa-ayqanu* (so they were certain). ﴿That they are about to fall into it⁠﴾ — *muwaqi'uha*, meaning *mukhalitûha* (mixing with it), *waqi'una fiha* (falling into it). ﴿And they will find no escape from it⁠﴾ — *masrifan*, meaning *insiraf* (turning away) or a place to which they might turn away.

﴿And We have certainly varied in this Qur'an for mankind every kind of example⁠﴾ — *min kulli mathal*, meaning every kind (*jins*) that they need. ﴿But man has ever been most contentious⁠﴾ — *yata'atta minhu al-jadal* (from which argument can arise). ﴿In dispute⁠﴾ — *khusuma bil-batil* (contention through falsehood); its being in the accusative is as a *tamyiz* (specification).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 55:

﴿And nothing prevented the people from believing﴾ from faith. ﴿When guidance had come to them﴾, namely the Messenger calling them and the clear Qur'an.

﴿And seek forgiveness from their Lord﴾ and seeking forgiveness from sins. ﴿Except that the custom of the former peoples should come upon them﴾ except that a demand, or an expectation, or a supposition that the custom of the former peoples should come upon them, namely annihilation, so the modifying noun (mudaf) was omitted and the modified noun (mudaf ilayh) was put in its place. ﴿Or that punishment should come upon them﴾, the punishment of the Hereafter. ﴿In front of them﴾ openly, face to face. The Kufans read (qubulan) with two dammas, and this is a dialect form of it, or the plural of qabil meaning kinds. It was also read with two fathas, and this too is a dialect form; it is said "I met him face to face" (muqabalatan), "qabalan," "qubulan," and "qabaliyyan." Its position is as a circumstantial accusative (hal) either from the pronoun or from ﴿the punishment﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 56:

﴿And We do not send the messengers except as bearers of good news and warners﴾ to the believers and the disbelievers. ﴿And those who disbelieve dispute with falsehood﴾ by demanding signs after the miracles have become manifest, and by asking about the story of the People of the Cave and the like, out of obstinacy. ﴿So that they may refute thereby﴾ so that they may remove by disputation ﴿the truth﴾ from its place and nullify it. It is derived from idhad al-qadam (dahd al-qadam), meaning the slipping of the foot, which is its slipping. This is what they say to the messengers: ﴿You are only human beings like us﴾ and ﴿If Allah had willed, He would have sent down angels﴾ and the like.

﴿And they take My signs﴾ meaning the Qur'an. ﴿And what they are warned of﴾ their being warned, or that with which they were warned of punishment. ﴿As a mockery﴾ as mockery. It has also been read as "huz'an" with a sukun, which is that which is mocked, according to both interpretations.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 57–58:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord﴾, by the Qur'an. ﴿but turns away from them﴾, not reflecting upon them and not taking heed by them. ﴿and forgets what his hands have sent forward﴾, of disbelief and sins, and does not contemplate their outcome. ﴿Indeed, We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾: this is a causal explanation (ta'lil) for their turning away and forgetting, namely that their hearts are sealed. ﴿lest they understand it﴾, that is, out of aversion to their understanding it. The pronoun is made masculine and singular in accordance with the meaning. ﴿and in their ears is deafness﴾, preventing them from listening to it as it ought to be listened to. ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will never be guided, then﴾, with certainty and not merely by way of imitation, because they neither understand nor hear. The word ﴿idhan﴾ (then), as you know, is a conditional particle and a response (jaza' wa jawab), addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ), on the presumption of his saying: "What is wrong with me that I do not call them?" His intense eagerness for their Islam indicates this.

﴿And your Lord is the Forgiving﴾, the one abounding in forgiveness. ﴿Full of mercy﴾, the one characterized by mercy. ﴿Were He to take them to account for what they earned, He would hasten their punishment for them﴾: this is cited as evidence for that, by His granting respite to Quraysh despite their excessive hostility toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿Rather, they have an appointment﴾, which is the Day of Badr, or the Day of Resurrection. ﴿They will not find besides Him any refuge﴾, any escape or shelter. It is said: "wa'ala" means he escaped, and "wa'ala ilayhi" means he sought refuge with him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 59:

﴿And those cities﴾ meaning the cities of ʿAd and Thamud and their like. "Tilka" (those) is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) follows. ﴿We destroyed them﴾ — or it is an implied object (maf'ul mudmar) explained by it, and "al-qura" (the cities) is its adjective (sifah). In either case, it is necessary to assume an omitted genitive construct (mudaf) in one of the two, so that there is a referent for the pronouns.

﴿When they did wrong﴾ like Quraysh, through denial, disputation, and various kinds of sins.

﴿And We appointed for their destruction a fixed time﴾ — a time for their destruction from which they would not be delayed by a single hour, nor brought forward. So let them take warning from them, and not be deceived by the postponement of punishment from them. Abu Bakr read "limahlakihim" with a fatha on the mim and the lam, meaning "li-halakihim" (for their perishing). Hafs read it with a kasra on the lam, analogizing it to the anomalous verbal nouns of the yafʿalu pattern, such as "al-marji'" (the return) and "al-mahid" (the menstruation).

(Allah says:) ﴿And when Moses said﴾, is implicitly governed by the verb "remember" (udhkur). ﴿to his young man﴾ refers to Yusha' ibn Nun ibn Afra'im ibn Yusuf, peace be upon them all, for he used to serve Moses and follow him, and for this reason he is called his "young man" (fata). It is also said that the word refers to his servant. ﴿I will not cease﴾ means "I will not stop travelling," and the predicate has been omitted because his situation indicates it, namely the journey. The phrase ﴿until I reach the meeting place of the two seas﴾ is consistent with this, since "until" (hatta) requires a goal to be attained. It is also possible that the original structure was "my journey will not cease until I reach," with "until I reach" as the predicate, so that the genitive noun (mudaf) was omitted and the noun in the genitive after it (mudaf ilayhi) took its place, which changed the pronoun and the verb. It is also possible that "I will not cease" (la abraḥ) means "I will not depart from what I am upon of travelling and seeking, and I will not leave it," in which case it does not require a predicate. The "meeting place of the two seas" (majma' al-bahrayn) is the confluence of the Persian and Roman seas on the eastern side, where he was promised a meeting with al-Khidr (the Green One). It is also said that the "two seas" are Moses and Khidr, peace be upon them both, for Moses was a sea of outward knowledge, and Khidr was a sea of inward knowledge.

It is recited as "mijma'" with a kasra on the mim, as an irregular form of the pattern "maf'il," like "mashriq" and "matla'". ﴿Or I will journey on for a long time﴾ means "or I will keep travelling for a long period." The meaning is that the goal will be reached either by arriving at the meeting place or by the passing of a long period. Or it means "until I reach it, unless I travel for a time during which I am certain I will miss the meeting place." A ḥuqub (long period) is an age; it is also said to be eighty years, and it is also said seventy.

It is related that Moses, peace be upon him, addressed the people after the destruction of the Copts and his entry into Egypt with an eloquent sermon, and he was impressed by it. He was asked, "Do you know anyone more knowledgeable than you?" He said, "No." So Allah revealed to him: "Rather, there is one more knowledgeable than you: Our servant al-Khidr, and he is at the meeting place of the two seas." Al-Khidr lived in the days of Afridun, and he was in the vanguard of Dhu'l-Qarnayn al-Akbar, and he remained until the time of Moses.

It is also said that Moses, peace be upon him, asked his Lord: "Which of Your servants is most beloved to You?" He said: "The one who remembers Me and does not forget Me." He said: "Which of Your servants is most just?" He said: "The one who judges by the truth and does not follow desire." He said: "Which of Your servants is most knowledgeable?" He said: "The one who seeks the knowledge of people for the sake of his own knowledge, hoping that he will hear a word that guides him to guidance or turns him back from destruction." He said: "If there is one among Your servants more knowledgeable than me, then guide me to him." He said: "The most knowledgeable than you is al-Khidr." He said: "Where shall I seek him?" He said: "On the shore, by the rock." He said: "How can I find him?" He said: "Take a fish in a basket, and wherever you lose it, he is there." So he said to his young man: "When you lose the fish, inform me." Then they set off, walking.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 61–62:

﴿When they reached the meeting place of the two of them﴾, that is, the meeting place of the two seas. "Between them" (*bayni-hima*) is an adverb of place (*zarf*) that has been annexed to what precedes it by extension (*ʿala al-ittisaʿ*), or in the sense of "junction" (*al-wasl*). ﴿They forgot their fish﴾: Musa, upon him be peace, forgot to seek it and to inquire about its condition, and Yusha' (Joshua) forgot to mention to him what he had seen of its life and of its falling into the sea.

It is narrated that Musa, upon him be peace, slept, and the roasted fish stirred, leapt into the sea, and this was a miracle for Musa or for al-Khidr.

It is also said that Yusha' performed ablution from the Spring of Life, water splashed onto the fish, it came to life, and it leapt into the water. It is said that they forgot to check on its matter and what would happen to it as a sign of attaining the sought-after goal. ﴿So it took its way into the sea, a tunnel﴾: the fish took its path into the sea as a passage, from the saying of Allah ﴿and one who moves freely by day﴾. It is also said that Allah held back the flow of the water over the fish so that it became like an arch over it. *Sarban* is in the accusative as a second object (*maf'ul thani*), and *fi al-bahr* ("in the sea") is a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of it or of the path; it is also permissible for it to be linked to *ittakhadha* ("took").

﴿When they had passed beyond it﴾, the meeting place of the two seas. ﴿He said to his attendant, "Bring us our morning meal; we have indeed suffered fatigue from this journey of ours"﴾. *Ghada'* is what we eat at midday. ﴿Nasaban﴾ is said to mean that he had not felt fatigue until he passed the appointed place; when he passed it and travelled through the night and the next day until noon, hunger and fatigue came upon him. It is also said that Musa did not become weary on any other journey, and this is supported by the restriction to the demonstrative "this" (*hadha*).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 61–62:

﴿When they reached the meeting place of the two of them﴾, that is, the meeting place of the two seas. "Between them" (*bayni-hima*) is an adverb of place (*zarf*) that has been annexed to what precedes it by extension (*ʿala al-ittisaʿ*), or in the sense of "junction" (*al-wasl*). ﴿They forgot their fish﴾: Musa, upon him be peace, forgot to seek it and to inquire about its condition, and Yusha' (Joshua) forgot to mention to him what he had seen of its life and of its falling into the sea.

It is narrated that Musa, upon him be peace, slept, and the roasted fish stirred, leapt into the sea, and this was a miracle for Musa or for al-Khidr.

It is also said that Yusha' performed ablution from the Spring of Life, water splashed onto the fish, it came to life, and it leapt into the water. It is said that they forgot to check on its matter and what would happen to it as a sign of attaining the sought-after goal. ﴿So it took its way into the sea, a tunnel﴾: the fish took its path into the sea as a passage, from the saying of Allah ﴿and one who moves freely by day﴾. It is also said that Allah held back the flow of the water over the fish so that it became like an arch over it. *Sarban* is in the accusative as a second object (*maf'ul thani*), and *fi al-bahr* ("in the sea") is a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of it or of the path; it is also permissible for it to be linked to *ittakhadha* ("took").

﴿When they had passed beyond it﴾, the meeting place of the two seas. ﴿He said to his attendant, "Bring us our morning meal; we have indeed suffered fatigue from this journey of ours"﴾. *Ghada'* is what we eat at midday. ﴿Nasaban﴾ is said to mean that he had not felt fatigue until he passed the appointed place; when he passed it and travelled through the night and the next day until noon, hunger and fatigue came upon him. It is also said that Musa did not become weary on any other journey, and this is supported by the restriction to the demonstrative "this" (*hadha*).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 63:

﴿He said: Did you see when we took shelter at the rock﴾ meaning: Did you see what troubled me when we took shelter? ﴿at the rock﴾ meaning the rock beside which Musa had slept.

It is also said that it is the rock that lies below the River of Oil (Nahr al-Zayt). ﴿For I forgot the fish﴾ I lost it, or I forgot to mention it because of what I had seen of it. ﴿And none caused me to forget it except Satan, that I should mention it﴾ meaning: none caused me to forget mentioning it except Satan. ﴿That I should mention it﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun. It was also read as "an adhkurakahu" (that I should mention it to you). This is an excuse for his forgetting, owing to Satan's preoccupying him with his whisperings. Although the situation was wondrous and such a thing should not be forgotten, yet since he had become accustomed to witnessing its like in the presence of Musa and had grown familiar with it, his concern for it diminished. Perhaps he forgot it because he was absorbed in contemplation and his inner being was drawn toward the sacred presence, owing to what had overtaken him from witnessing the dazzling signs. He attributed it to Satan either out of humbling himself, or because the inability of the faculties to bear both sides, and their being occupied with one to the neglect of the other, is counted a deficiency. ﴿And it took its way into the sea in a marvelous manner﴾ a marvelous way, which is that it became like a tunnel (sarab), or a marvelous taking. The second object is the adverbial phrase (zarf). It is also said that it is the verbal noun (masdar) of a suppressed verb, meaning he said at the end of his speech, or Musa said in reply, "Marvelous!" in amazement at that situation. It is also said that the verb belongs to Musa, meaning Musa took the path of the fish into the sea in a marvelous manner.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 64–65:

﴿He said: That is what we were seeking.﴾ That is, the matter of the fish. ﴿We were seeking﴾ means we were looking for, because it (the fish) is a sign of what was sought. ﴿So they both retraced their steps back along their track﴾ meaning they returned along the same road by which they had come. ﴿Retracing their steps﴾ means they were following their tracks, pursuing their trail closely, or, following the path step by step until they reached the rock.

﴿Then they found a servant of Our servants﴾ The majority hold that he was al-Khidr (peace be upon him), whose name was Balya ibn Malakan. It is said his name was al-Yasa', and it is said it was Ilyas. ﴿Whom We had given mercy from Us﴾ this is revelation and prophethood. ﴿And taught him knowledge from Our own presence﴾ that is, of what is specific to Us and cannot be known except by Our guidance, and it is the knowledge of the unseen.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 66:

﴿Musa said to him: "May I follow you on the condition that you teach me"﴾ "On the condition that you teach me" — this is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the kaf (the "you" of "I follow you").

﴿of what you have been taught of right guidance﴾ — knowledge that has rushd (rushd being the attainment of good). The two Basri readers (Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub) read it with two fathahs (rashadan), and both are dialectal variants, like al-bukhl and al-bakhal. It is the object of "teach me," and the returning pronoun object of "you have been taught" is omitted. Both are derived from 'alima, which takes one object. It is also permissible for rushdan to be a causative object (ʿillah) of "I follow you," or a verbal noun (masdar) with its verb supplied. Yet his prophethood and being the bearer of a sharia are not contradicted by his learning from another what was not a prerequisite in the matters of religion, for the Messenger ought to be more knowledgeable than those to whom he is sent regarding what he was sent with of the roots and branches of religion, not absolutely. He observed in this the utmost humility and courtesy: he belittled himself, asked permission to be his follower, and requested that he guide him and bestow upon him the favour of teaching some of what God had bestowed upon him.(p-288)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 67–68:

﴿He said: "Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me."﴾ He negated from him the ability to be patient in his company through several forms of emphasis, as if they were things that are neither valid nor sound, and he gave the reason for that and made excuse for it by his saying:

﴿"And how can you have patience over that which you do not encompass in knowledge?"﴾ That is: and how can you be patient, while you are a prophet, with matters whose outward forms are objectionable and whose inner realities your knowledge does not encompass? And khubran (in knowledge) is either a specification (tamyiz) or a verbal noun (masdar), because "lam tuhit bihi" (you did not encompass it) carries the meaning of "lam tukhbar bihi" (you were not informed of it).

He said, "You will find me, God willing, patient with you, not objecting to you." ﴿And I will not disobey any command of yours.﴾ This is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to ﴿patient﴾, meaning: you will find me patient and not disobedient. Alternatively, it is conjoined to ﴿you will find me﴾.

Making the promise conditional on God's will is either for blessing (tayammun), and his breaking it out of forgetfulness does not impair his infallibility (ʿiṣmah). Or it is because he knew the difficulty of the matter, since witnessing corruption and being patient in the face of what is contrary to what is customary is severe, so there is no breaking of the promise. In this there is evidence that the actions of servants occur by the will of God the Exalted.

He said, "If you follow me, then do not ask me about anything." That is, do not open with me by asking about anything you have disapproved of in me while not knowing the reason for its soundness. ﴿Until I myself mention it to you.﴾ That is, until I begin to explain it to you. Nafiʿ and Ibn ʿAmir read ﴿fa-la tasalnnī﴾ with the heavy nun (al-nūn al-thaqīlah, the doubled nun of emphasis).
