﴿So they set off﴾ along the shore, seeking a ship. ﴿Until, when they boarded the ship, he tore it open﴾. Al-Khadir took an axe and tore open the ship by prying out two of its planks. ﴿He said, "Have you torn it open to drown its people?"﴾ Tearing it open is the cause of water entering it, which leads to the drowning of its people.

It was also recited as «لِتُغَرِّقَ» with the doubled ra' (tashdid), for intensification. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited «لِيَغْرَقَ أهْلُها» (so that its people would drown), attributing the verb to "its people." ﴿You have certainly done a dreadful thing﴾: you have committed a grave matter, from the verb «أمُرَ» meaning "to become great" when the matter grows serious.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 73:

﴿He said: Do not hold me to account for what I forgot⦆ — that is, for that which I forgot, or for something I forgot, namely his instruction not to object to him, or for my forgetting it. This is an excuse by means of forgetting, which he presented in the form of a prohibition against being held to account, while the preventive factor for it (i.e., the excuse) remains in place. It has also been said that by "forgetting" he meant "leaving", i.e., do not hold me to account for what I left of your instruction the first time. It has also been said that it is one of the indirect forms of speech (ma'arid al-kalam), and that what is meant is something else he had forgotten.

﴿And do not burden me with hardship in my affair﴾ — and do not cover me with hardship in my affair through harassment and holding me to account for what was forgotten, for that would make following you difficult for me. The word ﴿hardship﴾ is the second object of tur'hiq (to burden/overwhelm), for it is said: rahiqahu (he overtook him) when it overtook him, and arhaqahu iyyahu (he made it overtake him with it). It has been read as (ʿusuran), with two dammas.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 74:

﴿So they set out﴾, that is, after they had left the boat. ﴿Until, when they met a boy, he killed him﴾. It was said that he broke his neck; it was said that he struck his head against the wall; it was said that he laid him down and slaughtered him. The fa' (the particle of sequence, fa) indicates that as soon as he met him, he killed him without deliberation or investigating his condition. Hence: ﴿He said: "Have you killed a pure soul without its having killed anyone?"﴾, that is, one pure of sins. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ruways from Ya'qub read "zakiyyatan" (زاكيةً), but the first (zakiyyatan, زكيةً) is more eloquent. Abu 'Amr said: the zakiyah (زاكية) is the one who has never sinned at all, while the zakiyyah (زكية) is the one who sinned and then was forgiven. Perhaps he (al-Baydawi's source or the reading) preferred the first for this reason: that the boy was young and had not reached puberty; or that he did not see that the boy had committed a sin that warranted his killing. Or [the meaning is]: "You have killed a soul so that it is retaliated against with you." He thereby indicated that killing is permitted only as a hadd (prescribed punishment) or as qisas (retaliation), and both of these conditions are absent. Perhaps the change in arrangement, by making the breaking of the boat a conditional response, and Musa's objection (peace be upon him) being stated as a separate sentence in the first case, while in the second case killing him is part of the conditional clause and his objection is the response, is because killing is more heinous and objecting to it is more fitting; so it deserved to be made the main point of the speech. For this reason he elaborated it with his saying: ﴿Indeed you have come up with a dreadful thing﴾, that is, a denounced thing. Nafi', in the narration of Qalun and Warsh, Ibn 'Amir, Ya'qub and Abu Bakr read "nukuran" (نُكُرًا) with two dammas.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 75–76:

﴿He said: "Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?"﴾ He added "for you" (lakа) as a sharp rebuke with reproach for rejecting the condition (wasiyyah), and as a branding of you with lack of steadiness and patience, since his disapproval and objection were repeated, and he did not heed the reminder the first time, so that he increased his objection the second time.

﴿He said: "If I ask you about anything after this, then do not keep me as a companion."﴾ That is, if I ask to accompany you. And in the reading of Ya'qub, "fa-la tasbihni" (then do not keep me company), meaning: do not make me your companion. ﴿Indeed you have received from me an excuse﴾: you have found an excuse from my side, since I opposed you three times.

And from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "May Allah have mercy on my brother Musa; he was modest, so he said that. Had he remained with his companion, he would have seen the most wondrous of wonders."

Nafi' read (min ladunni) with the nun vowelled, dispensing with the supporting nun (nun al-di'amah), as in the verse: "qidni min nasri al-habibayni qudan" (suffice me from the help of the two beloveds, a measure). Abu Bakr read (ladhni) with the nun vowelled and the dad silent, from ʿadhd (support).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 77:

﴿So they set out, until when they came upon the people of a town﴾ — the town of Antioch (Antakiyya); it is also said Ubulla (Ubulla of Basra), and it is also said Bajrawan of Armenia. ﴿They asked its people for food, but they refused to host them﴾. It is read ﴿yudayyifuhuma﴾ (they would host them), from aḍāfahu. It is said ḍāfahu when one alights with him as a guest, and aḍāfahu and ḍayyafahu mean he lodged him. The basic root meaning is inclination; it is said ḍāfa al-sahmu ʿan al-gharaḍ (the arrow veered away from the target) when it inclines. ﴿They found in it a wall that was about to collapse﴾ — it was close to falling. So the word "will (irāda)" is used metaphorically for "approaching," just as "concern (hamm)" and "resolve (ʿazm)" are used for it. The poet said:

"The spear wills (yurīdu) the chest of Abu Barāʾ, / and turns away from the blood of Banu ʿUqayl."

And he said:

"Indeed a time that gathers my scattered affairs with a group... / is a time that intends (yahummu) goodness."

Inqaḍḍa is of the form infaʿala, from qaḍaḍtuhu, when I broke it; from it comes the swooping (inqiḍāḍ) of birds and stars because of their falling. Or it is of the form afʿala, from the naqḍ (breaking).

It was also read ﴿an yanqaḍḍa﴾ and ﴿an yanqāṣṣa﴾ with the unpointed ṣād, from inqāṣat al-sinn, when the tooth splits lengthwise. ﴿So he set it upright﴾ — by rebuilding it, or by propping it up with a pillar he supported it with; it is also said he wiped it with his hand and it stood. It is also said he demolished it and rebuilt it. ﴿He said: "If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it."﴾ This is an incitement to accept a fee so that they might be sustained by it, or an allusion that it was superfluous, because of the negation implied in "law" (lawa). It is as if, when he saw their deprivation, the touch of need, and his own preoccupation with what did not concern him, he could not restrain himself. Ittakhadha is of the form iftaʿala from takhidha, like ittabaʿa from tabiʿa, and it is not from akhadh (taking) according to the Basran grammarians. Ibn Kathir and the two Basrans read "latakhidhta" (you would have taken), meaning "la-akhadhat" (she would have taken). Ibn Kathir, Yaʿqub and Hafs made the dal explicit, and the rest assimilated it.

Al-Baydawi, Anwar al-Tanzil, on surah 18, verse 78:

﴿He said: "This is the parting between me and you."﴾ The demonstrative refers either to the parting that was promised in his words ﴿so do not accompany me﴾, or to the third objection, or to the time; that is, this objection is the cause of our parting, or this time is its time. The attribution of "parting" (firaq) to "between" (bayn) is an attribution of the verbal noun (masdar) to a adverbial noun of place/time (zarf) in an extended usage (ʿala al-ittisaʿ), and it has been read in the original form (ʿala al-asl), [i.e., as firaqu baynī wa-baynika without the extension]. ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that which you could not bear with patience﴾ — that is, with the inner reality (al-khabar al-batin) concerning that which you could not endure patiently, because its outward appearance was objectionable.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 79:

﴿As for the ship, it belonged to poor people who worked on the sea﴾ (masakin, i.e. needy people). This is evidence that the word miskin (poor) is applied to one who possesses something if it does not suffice him. It has been said that they were called masakin because of their inability to repel the king, or because of their disabilities, for the ship belonged to ten brothers: five of them were disabled (zamna) and five worked on the sea. ﴿So I wished to damage it﴾, that is, to make it defective. ﴿And there was behind them a king﴾, in front of them or behind them, and their return was to him. His name was Jalanda ibn Karkar, and it has been said that he was Minwar ibn Jalandayy al-Azdi. ﴿Who seized every ship by force﴾ from its owners.

The proper order of the discourse would have been for the statement ﴿So I wished to damage it﴾ to come after the statement ﴿And there was behind them a king﴾, because the wish to make it defective is caused by fear of forcible seizure. It was placed first for emphasis, or because the cause was the combination of two matters, fear of forcible seizure and the poverty of the owners; he arranged it according to the stronger and more pressing of the two parts, and then followed it with the other as a qualification and completion. It has also been read as ﴿every ship that was sound (saliha)﴾, and the meaning is the same (i.e., the reading implies that the king seized ships that were sound).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 80–81:

﴿And as for the boy, his parents were believers, and We feared that he would burden them with rebellion and disbelief.﴾ That is, that he would overwhelm them (an-yughshiyahuma). ﴿Rebellion and disbelief﴾: by his ingratitude toward their blessing, which would bring evil upon them; or he would join his rebellion and disbelief to their faith, so that two believers and a rebellious disbeliever would be gathered in one house; or he would infect them with his affliction, so that they would apostatize through his misguidance; or they would help him in his rebellion and disbelief out of love for him. He feared this only because God Most High had informed him of it. And on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both: "Najdah al-Haruri wrote to him asking how he [Khidr] had killed [the boy] when the Prophet ﷺ had forbidden the killing of children. So he wrote back to him: 'If you have known of the condition of children what the scholar of Musa knew, then you may kill.'" It has been recited as "fakhafa rabbaka" (so he feared your Lord), meaning: he disliked it, as one who fears the evil of its outcome. It is also possible that his saying ﴿we feared﴾ is a narration of the words of God, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿So We desired that their Lord would replace him for them with one better than him﴾: that He would grant them a child better than him. ﴿Purity﴾: cleanliness from sins and bad character. ﴿And nearer in compassion﴾: more merciful and tender toward his parents. It is said that they had a daughter, who was married to a prophet, and she bore him a prophet through whom God guided a nation of the nations. Nafiʿ and Abu ʿAmr recited ﴿yubdilahuma﴾ with the doubled letter (tashdid), and Ibn ʿAmir, Yaʿqub and ʿAsim recited ﴿ruḥman﴾ with the single letter (takhfif). Its accusative case is that of specification (tamyiz), and the governing element is the comparative form (ism at-tafdil). Likewise ﴿zakatan﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 82:

﴿As for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city.﴾ It is said that their names were Asram and Sarim, and the name of the murdered boy was Jaysur.

﴿Beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾ of gold and silver. This has been related as a marfu' (traced back to the Prophet ﷺ) report. The censure of hoarding in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver﴾ applies to one who does not pay their zakat and the other rights attached to them. It is also said that it was from books of knowledge. It is also said that there was a tablet of gold on which was written: "I marvel at one who believes in destiny, how he grieves; I marvel at one who believes in provision, how he toils; I marvel at one who believes in reckoning, how he is heedless; I marvel at one who believes in death, how he rejoices; I marvel at one who knows the world and its turning with its people, how he finds rest in it. There is no god but Allah; Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." ﴿And their father was righteous﴾ is an indication that their guardianship of the treasure was due to his righteousness. It is said that between them and the father in whose merit they were protected there were seven generations, and he was a wanderer, and his name was Kashih.

﴿So your Lord desired that they should reach their maturity﴾, that is, the age of puberty and full judgment. ﴿And that they should extract their treasure as a mercy from your Lord﴾ — being shown mercy from your Lord. It may be that it is a cause or a verbal noun for "desired," since the desire for good is a mercy. It is also said that it is connected to an omitted element, its estimated sense being: "I did what I did as a mercy from your Lord." Perhaps the attribution of the desire first to himself is because he was the one directly carrying out the damaging of the wall; second to God and to himself, because the replacement came through the destruction of the boy and God's creating a substitute for him; and third to God alone, because he had no part in the boys reaching maturity. Or, because the first is evil in itself, the third is good, and the second is mixed. Or, because of the differing state of the knower in regard to turning toward intermediaries.

﴿And I did not do it﴾, that is, I did not do what you saw, ﴿of my own accord﴾, that is, by my own opinion; rather I did it by the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is based on the principle that when two harms conflict, one must bear the lesser of them to avert the greater; this is a foundational principle, though the sacred laws differ in its details.

﴿That is the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience﴾, that is, what you could not endure. The letter ta' has been dropped for lightness.

Among the benefits of this story: a person should not be vain about his knowledge, nor hasten to deny what he does not find good, for perhaps there is a secret in it that he does not know; that he should persevere in learning and humble himself before the teacher, and observe good manners in return; and that he should alert the wrongdoer to his wrong and pardon him until his persistence is confirmed, and then part from him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 83:

﴿They ask you about Dhu al-Qarnayn.﴾ He means Iskandar (Alexander) the Roman, king of Persia and Rome. It is also said that he was (called so because of) the East and the West, and for this reason he was named Dhu al-Qarnayn (the Two-Horned). Or (it is because) he traversed the two horns of the world, its East and its West. It is also said that he was named so because two generations of people passed away during his days. It is said that he had two horns, meaning two braids (of hair). It is also said that there were two horns on his crown. It is possible that he was given this epithet for his bravery, just as a ram (kabsh) is called so for a brave man, as if he gores his peers. There is disagreement about his prophethood, while there is agreement on his faith and righteousness. As for those who asked, they were the Jews, who asked him as a test, or the polytheists of Makkah. ﴿Say: I will recite to you a remembrance from him.﴾ The address is to the questioners, and the pronoun (in "from him") refers to Dhu al-Qarnayn. It is also said that it refers to Allah.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 84:

﴿Indeed, We established him firmly in the earth﴾, meaning: We gave him power over his affairs in disposing of it however he wished, so the object is omitted. ﴿And We gave him of every thing﴾, meaning: whatever he intended and pursued. ﴿A means﴾, meaning: a connection that brings him to it, of knowledge, power, and equipment.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 85–86:

﴿So he followed a means﴾, i.e., he intended to reach the west, so he followed a means that would bring him to it. The Kufans and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿atba'a﴾ with an elided alif (ʾatbaʿa, "he followed") and the ta' lightened (mukhaffafa), i.e., read as ʾatbaʿa rather than ittaba'a.

﴿Until, when he reached the setting-place of the sun, he found it setting in a spring of murky water (ḥamiʾa)﴾, i.e., having mud from ḥamiʾat al-bi'r (the well became muddy) when it becomes full of ḥamʾa (mud). Ibn 'Amir, Ḥamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read ﴿ḥāmiyatan﴾, i.e., hot. There is no contradiction between them, since the spring may combine both qualities; or it is read ﴿ḥimyatan﴾, its yā' being a substitution for the hamza because of the kasra before it. Perhaps he reached the shore of the Ocean (al-Muḥīṭ) and saw it thus, since there was nothing within the range of his sight except the water; for this reason he said ﴿he found it setting﴾ and did not say ﴿it was setting﴾. It is said that Ibn 'Abbas heard Mu'awiya reading ﴿ḥāmiyatan﴾, so he said ﴿ḥamiʾatan﴾. Mu'awiya then sent to Ka'b al-Ahbar: "How do you find the sun setting?" He said: "In water and mud; thus do we find it in the Torah."

﴿And he found near it﴾, near that spring, ﴿a people﴾. It is said that their clothing was the hides of wild animals and their food was what the sea cast up, and they were disbelievers. So God gave him the choice between punishing them or calling them to faith, as He related by His saying: ﴿We said, "O Dhu'l-Qarnayn, either you punish them﴾, i.e., by killing them for their disbelief, ﴿or you adopt among them goodness﴾, by guidance and teaching the laws. It is also said that God gave him the choice between killing and taking captives, and called the latter "goodness" in contrast to killing. The first view is supported by His saying:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 87–88:

﴿He said: "As for him who does wrong, we will punish him; then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him with a terrible punishment."﴾ That is, he chose the call (to faith) and said: "As for him whose call has been rejected and who wrongs himself by persisting in his disbelief, or who continues in his wrongdoing, which is polytheism, we will punish him, I and those with me, in this world by killing; then Allah will punish him in the Hereafter with a dreadful punishment such as He has never inflicted the like of."

﴿But as for him who believes and does righteous deeds﴾ which is what faith requires. ﴿he will have a reward, the best﴾ in both abodes. ﴿the best﴾ means his action is the best. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Hafs read jaza'an (reward) with tanwin and in the accusative, as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning: "for him is the best recompense, being rewarded with it," or as an accusative of the verbal noun (maṣdar) for an implied verb, meaning: "He will reward with it a reward," or as a specification (tamyīz). It is also read in the accusative without tanwin, the tanwin having been dropped because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters (iltiqā' al-sākinayn), and with tanwin in the nominative, in which case it is the subject (mubtada'), and "the best" (al-ḥusnā) is its substitute (badal). It is possible that the two occurrences of "as for" (amma) are for division rather than choice, meaning: "let your attitude toward them be either punishment or kindness; the first is for him who persists in disbelief, and the second for him who repents from it." Allah's calling out to him, if he was a prophet, is by revelation (waḥy), and if he was other than a prophet, by inspiration (ilhām) or through the tongue of a prophet.

﴿And we will speak to him of Our command﴾ with what We order. ﴿with ease﴾ easily, facilitated, not burdensome; its estimated form is "possessing ease." It is also read with two ḍammas (yusran).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 89–91:

﴿Then he followed a course﴾ Then he followed a route that brought him to the east (al-mashriq).

﴿Until, when he reached the rising-place of the sun﴾ meaning the place where the sun first rises upon the inhabited part of the earth (ma'murat al-ard). It is also read with a fatha on the lam, on the assumption of an omitted genitive construction, i.e., "the place of the rising of the sun," since it is a noun of place (masdar). ﴿He found it rising over a people for whom We had made no shelter against it﴾ meaning no covering of clothing or building; either their land does not hold buildings, or they took caves (asrab) in place of buildings.

﴿Thus⦆ i.e., the matter of Dhu al-Qarnayn is as We have described it in the loftiness of his position and the expanse of his kingship, or his dealing with them is like his dealing with the people of the west, in terms of choice and discretion. It may also be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun for "found" or "make," or an adjective of "a people," meaning over a people like that tribe over whom the sun sets in disbelief and judgment. ﴿And We had encompassed what was with him﴾ of soldiers, equipment, provisions, and means. ﴿In knowledge﴾ knowledge that encompassed its outward and hidden aspects. The meaning is that the multitude of these things reached a degree that none could encompass except the knowledge of the Subtle, the All-Aware.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 92–93:

﴿Then he followed a means﴾ meaning a third path, running between the east and the west, taking a course from the south toward the north.

﴿Until, when he reached between the two barriers﴾ between the two mountains, between which he built the barrier. They are the two mountains of Armenia and Adharbayjan. It is also said they are two lofty mountains at the far north, at the farthest end of the land of the Turks, behind which are Ya'juj and Ma'juj. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr and Ya'qub read (بَيْنَ السُّدَّيْنِ) with a damma, and both are two dialects. It is also said that the form with a damma refers to what Allah created, and the form with a fatha refers to what people constructed, because it is originally a verbal noun (masdar) which was used as a name for a deed that people perform. It is also said the reverse is true. Here, بَيْنَ is the object (maf'ul bihi) (p-293), and it is among the flexibly inflected adverbials (al-zuruf al-mutasarrifah).

﴿He found, beside them, a people who scarcely understood any speech﴾ because of the strangeness of their language and the scarcity of their understanding. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read «لا يُفْقِهُونَ» (la yufqihuna), meaning they do not make the listener understand their speech, nor do they clarify it, due to their stammering in it.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 94–96:**

﴿They said, "O Dhul-Qarnayn!"﴾ Its translator (*mutarjim*) said: In the codex (*mushaf*) of Ibn Mas'ud it reads: "He said, *al-ladhina min dunihim*" (those who are beside them).

﴿Indeed, Ya'juj and Ma'juj﴾ are two tribes from the descendants of Yafith ibn Nuh (Japheth son of Noah). It is also said that Ya'juj are from the Turks and Ma'juj from the mountain. They are two non-Arabic names (*ism a'jami*), as shown by their not taking tanwin (*man' al-sarf*). It is also said they are Arabic, derived from *aja* (أجّ), meaning the ostrich (*zalim*) when it runs quickly. Their original form has a hamza, as Asim recited, and their declension is prevented for definiteness (*ta'rif*) and feminine form (*ta'nith*).

﴿Causing corruption in the land﴾ means in our land, through killing, destruction, and the ruin of crops. It is said that they would go out in the spring and leave nothing green without eating it, nor anything dry without carrying it off. It is also said that they used to eat people.

﴿Shall we then set aside for you a tribute﴾ means a payment that we bring out from our wealth. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *kharajan* (خَراجًا), and both forms have the same meaning, like *nawl* and *nawal* (النَّوْل والنَّوال). It is also said that *al-kharaj* refers to land tax and protection-tax (*dhimma*), while *al-kharj* is the verbal noun.

﴿On condition that you set up a barrier between us and them﴾ which would block their coming out against us. Whoever read the two *sudd*s with a *damma* other than Hamzah and al-Kisa'i has also read it that way.

﴿He said, "That in which my Lord has established me is better"﴾ meaning: that in which He has made me firmly established (*makin*) in wealth and dominion is better than what you offer me as tribute, and I have no need of it. Ibn Kathir read *makkanani* (مَكَّنَنِي) according to the original form.

﴿So help me with strength﴾ means with the strength of workers, or with the tools by which I can gain strength.

﴿I will set up between you and them a rampart (*radman*)﴾ meaning a strong, fortified barrier, which is greater than a *sadd*. From the saying *thawbun mudarram* (ثَوْبٌ مُرَدَّمٌ), when it is patches upon patches.

﴿Bring me blocks of iron﴾ meaning its pieces; a *zubra* is a large piece. This does not contradict his refusal of the tribute and his limiting himself to assistance, because *al-iti'a* (giving) here means handing over. This is supported by Abu Bakr's reading *radman i'tuni* (رَدْمًا ائْتُونِي), with the tanwin of *radman* kasra'd and the hamza connected, meaning "come to me with blocks of iron" (جِيئُونِي بِزُبَرِ الحَدِيدِ), with the preposition *ba'* omitted, as in *amartuka al-khayr* (أمَرْتُكَ الخَيْرَ). Also, giving the tools is part of helping with strength, unlike the tribute for the work.

﴿Until, when he had leveled up between the two cliffs﴾ meaning between the two sides of the mountains, by stacking them in layers. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and the two Basran readers read it with two *damma*s; Abu Bakr read it with *damma* on the *sad* and sukun on the *dal*. It was also read with *fatha* on the *sad* and *damma* on the *dal*. All of these are dialectal forms of *al-sadaf* (الصَّدَف), which means inclination, because each of the two sides is separate from the other. From it comes *al-tasadduf* (التَّصادُف), meaning facing one another.

﴿He said, "Blow!"﴾ meaning he said to the workers, "Blow into the bellows (*akwar*) and the iron."

﴿Until, when he had made it﴾ meaning he made the thing blown into it.

﴿Fire﴾ like fire through heating.

﴿He said, "Bring me, that I may pour over it molten copper"﴾ meaning: bring me molten copper (*qitran*), that is, molten brass, so that I may pour it over it. The first object was omitted because the second indicates it. The Basran grammarians used this as evidence that when two governing verbs point to one object, it is better to make the second one govern it, since if *qitran* were the object of *atuni*, the object of *afrigh* would have to be implied, which would cause confusion. Hamzah and Abu Bakr read *qala atuni* (قالَ أتُونِي) with the hamza connected.

﴿Until, when he had made it﴾ meaning he made the thing blown into it.

﴿Fire﴾ like fire through heating.

﴿He said, "Bring me, that I may pour over it molten copper"﴾ meaning: bring me molten copper (*qitran*), that is, molten brass, so that I may pour it over it. ﴿So they were not able﴾, with the *tā'* dropped (*fa-mā istaṭā'ū*), to avoid the meeting of two close consonants. ﴿That they could make it manifest﴾: that they could climb over it, because of its height and its smoothness.

It was said that he dug for the foundation until he reached water, and he made it of rock and molten copper, and the building was of blocks of iron, with wood and charcoal between them, until it reached the level of the tops of the two mountains. Then he placed the bellows until it became like fire, and molten copper was poured over it, so it mixed and its parts stuck together and it became a solid mountain.

He said: "This is a mercy from my Lord. But when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level with the ground; and the promise of my Lord is ever true."

Let me restate this carefully and fully, following your instructions.

"He said: 'This' — this wall, or the decrees (al-aqdar) regarding its leveling — 'is a mercy from my Lord' upon His servants. 'But when the promise of my Lord comes' — the time of His promise regarding the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj, or the establishment of the Hour, by the Day of Resurrection drawing near. 'He will make it levelled' — made crushed, spread out, made even with the ground. It is a verbal noun (masdar) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), and from it comes the phrase jamal adakk (a camel with a flat, level hump). Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 102:

﴿Do those who disbelieve think﴾ (i.e., do they suppose), and the interrogative is for denunciation. ﴿that they may take My servants﴾ (i.e., their taking) the angels and the Messiah.

﴿as protectors besides Me﴾ — as deities who benefit them. Or: "I will not punish them because of it," so the second object is omitted, as the predicate is omitted when there is an indicator. Or: "that they may take" fills the place of both objects. It is also read: "Afahasiba alladhina kafaru" (Do those who disbelieve reckon), meaning: is it enough for them for salvation? And "inna" with what is within its scope is in the nominative case, as the subject of "hasiba," since when the attributive clause relies on the interrogative particle it equals the verb in governing; or it is its predicate. ﴿Indeed, We have prepared Hell for the disbelievers as a nuzul﴾ — that which is prepared for a guest. In this there is mockery and an alert that, beyond it, they will have punishment so that what they have is considered trivial in comparison.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 103–104:

﴿Say: Shall We inform you of those who are the greatest losers in deeds?﴾ It is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), and it is in the plural because it is one of the nouns of the agents (ism al-fa'il), or because of the variety of their deeds.

﴿Those whose effort is lost in the life of this world﴾: it was wasted and became void because of their disbelief and self-conceit, like the monks (al-Rahabina). Its place in i'rab is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject (khabar mahdhuf), since it is the answer to the question; or in the genitive as an apposition (badal); or in the accusative as a dispraise (dhamm).

﴿And they think that they are doing good work﴾: through their self-conceit and their belief that they are upon the truth.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verses 105–106:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 109:

﴿Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord⁠﴾ — that with which they are written. Midad (ink) is the name of that which supplies a thing, like ink for the inkwell and oil for the lamp.

﴿for the words of my Lord⁠﴾ — the words of His knowledge and wisdom. ﴿the sea would be exhausted⁠﴾ — the kind of sea would be exhausted, by His command, because every body is finite. ﴿before the words of my Lord are exhausted⁠﴾ — for they are infinite and are not exhausted, like His knowledge. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "tanfada" with the ya' (yanfada). ﴿Even if We brought the like of it⁠﴾ — the like of the sea that exists. ﴿as a supplement⁠﴾ — an increase and an aid, because the totality of finite things is finite. Rather, the totality of bodies that enter into existence cannot be anything but finite, by the decisive proofs that dimensions are finite, and what is finite is certainly exhausted before what is infinite is exhausted.

It is also read "yanfada" with the ya' and "madadan" with a kasrah on the mim, the plural of madda (a supply), which is what the writer draws upon for his ink (midad). The occasion of its revelation was that the Jews said: "In your Book, ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has indeed been given much good⁠﴾ [2:269], and you recite ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little⁠﴾ [17:85]."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 18, verse 110:

﴿Say: I am only a human being like you.﴾ I do not claim to encompass His words. ﴿It is revealed to me that your God is one God.﴾ And by this I am distinguished from you. ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord﴾ hopes for a good meeting with Him, or fears a bad meeting with Him. ﴿let him do righteous deeds﴾ that Allah approves of. ﴿And let him not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾ by showing off to Him (riya') or by seeking a reward from him.

It is narrated that Jundub ibn Zuhayr said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I perform an act for the sake of Allah, but when it is seen, it pleases me." He said: "Allah does not accept what is associated with others in it." Then this verse was revealed confirming him. And from him (ﷺ), peace be upon him: "Beware of the lesser shirk (shirk asghar, minor association with Allah)." They said: "And what is the lesser shirk?" He said: "Riya' (showing off)."

The verse comprises the two essentials of knowledge and action, namely tawhid (the oneness of God) and sincerity (ikhlas) in obedience.

And if his bed is in Mecca, it will be for him a light shining from his bed up to the Bayt al-Ma'mur (the frequented house in heaven), and filling that light are angels who send blessings upon him until he wakes."
